You are screening bibliographic records for the DESTINY repository, which captures the global
literature at the intersection of climate change — including its impacts, mitigation, and
adaptation — and health.

Decide whether this record should be included in the repository -- true = INCLUDE, false =
EXCLUDE -- according to the criteria below.

Decide only from the title, abstract, and metadata provided; do not use outside information to
fill gaps. Neither climate nor health need be the paper's primary topic, and the exact words
need not appear. Judge each record on its own; do not assume a prevalence. If the abstract is
missing or garbled, do your best with what is present.

INCLUDE a record when it has BOTH a CLIMATE COMPONENT and a HEALTH COMPONENT. Each may be stated
explicitly or be directly inferable from what the study addresses. When both are plausibly
present, lean toward INCLUDE. EXCLUDE when either is absent, or present only incidentally or
speculatively.

------------------------------------------------------------
CLIMATE COMPONENT — the record substantively addresses at least one of:

- A climate or weather factor: climate change or variability; a weather/climate variable
  (temperature, precipitation, humidity, wind, drought, heat, cold); a climate-related extreme
  event (heatwave, flood, drought, storm, cyclone, storm surge, wildfire); a greenhouse gas or
  other climate-forcing agent (CO2, methane, N2O, black carbon, and particulate matter --
  including wildfire, peatland, and biomass-burning smoke and haze, which are largely black
  carbon and other combustion particulates); or fossil fuels and their use.

- A mitigation action: an intervention, technology, practice, or policy that reduces or removes
  greenhouse-gas emissions, or reduces or replaces fossil-fuel use.

- An adaptation action: preparedness, resilience, vulnerability reduction, or climate-risk
  management against climate-related hazards -- including research that generates the evidence
  for these (projections, risk assessments, hazard models, monitoring, decision-support).

"Substantive" means the factor is measured, modelled, analysed, used as an exposure or outcome,
or is the target of the intervention -- not merely named in passing. A single chemical studied
only in vitro, or a substance present for a non-climate reason (a drug, a toxicant, an accident
hazard), is not a climate component.

------------------------------------------------------------
HEALTH COMPONENT -- the record substantively connects to human health or health systems. The
connection may be an adverse effect or risk, OR the protection, improvement, or promotion of human
physical or mental health or wellbeing (health is not only the absence of harm). It is established
via either:

- A direct human-health outcome: disease, morbidity, mortality, injury, respiratory or
  cardiovascular health, human exposure, mental health, occupational or public health, or
  healthcare and health-system capacity; OR

- A recognised climate-health exposure pathway, where the health effect follows from the
  exposure even if no clinical outcome is named:
  - Air quality (particulate matter, ground-level ozone, wildfire/biomass smoke and haze, dust,
    pollen) -> respiratory and cardiovascular health;
  - Extreme weather (floods, droughts, storms, storm surges) -> injury, death, mental health, care
    disruption
  - Food produced for human consumption (food crops, livestock, dairy, fisheries) -> nutrition,
    food security, foodborne disease;
  - Heat, cold, or UV -> heat illness, cold injury, skin and eye damage;
  - Psychosocial impact of climate change or climate-related disasters (distress, trauma, grief
    or loss, recovery and coping) -> mental health;
  - Vector ecology (mosquitoes, ticks, rodents, sandflies) -> vector-borne disease;
  - Water as a human-health hazard or resource (harmful algal blooms and cyanobacteria,
    waterborne pathogens, contamination, or water people use or drink) -> waterborne disease.

literature at the intersection of climate change -- including its impacts, mitigation, and
adaptation -- and health.

Decide whether this record should be included -- true = INCLUDE, false = EXCLUDE.

This is a HIGH-RECALL screen: the goal is to capture every record with any plausible connection
to climate and health. When a qualifying connection is plausibly present, or you are uncertain,
answer INCLUDE. Reserve EXCLUDE for records with no plausible connection.

Decide only from the title, abstract, and metadata provided. Neither climate nor health need be
the paper's primary topic, and the exact words need not appear. If the abstract is missing or
garbled, do your best with what is present.

A CLIMATE FACTOR is any of: climate change or variability; a weather/climate variable
(temperature, precipitation, humidity, wind, drought, heat, cold); a climate-related extreme
event (heatwave, flood, drought, storm, cyclone, storm surge, wildfire); a greenhouse gas or
other climate-forcing agent (CO2, methane, N2O, black carbon, and particulate matter --
including wildfire and biomass-burning smoke and haze); or fossil fuels and their extraction, production, refining, combustion, or use.

INCLUDE the record if ANY ONE of the following routes is plausibly present:

ROUTE 1 -- CLIMATE-HEALTH IMPACT: a climate factor is connected to human health, wellbeing, or
health systems. The connection may be an adverse effect or risk, OR the protection, improvement,
or promotion of physical or mental health or wellbeing (health is not only the absence of harm).
It may be a direct outcome (disease, morbidity, mortality, injury, respiratory or cardiovascular
health, mental health, human exposure, occupational or public health, healthcare capacity) OR an
indirect climate-health exposure pathway: air quality (particulate matter, ozone, wildfire/
biomass smoke and haze, dust, pollen); extreme weather (floods, storms, surges) affecting people,
settlements, or the structures and infrastructure they depend on; food produced for human
consumption (crops, livestock, dairy, fisheries); heat, cold, or UV; the psychosocial dimension
and wellbeing of people facing the climate crisis or disasters; vector ecology; or water as a
human-health hazard or resource (algal blooms and cyanobacteria, waterborne pathogens,
contamination, or water people use or drink). Connections may be explicit or plausibly inferred.

ROUTE 2 -- MITIGATION ACTION: the record studies any action, technology, practice, or policy
that reduces or removes greenhouse-gas emissions, or reduces or replaces fossil-fuel use. Any
mitigation action qualifies on its own; a separate health outcome is not required.

ROUTE 3 -- ADAPTATION ACTION: the record studies, or generates evidence for (projections, risk
assessments, hazard models, monitoring, decision-support), any preparedness, resilience,
vulnerability-reduction, disaster-risk-reduction, or climate-risk-management action that helps
protect people, human settlements, ecosystems people depend on, or health systems from
climate-related hazards.

Also INCLUDE records that couple climate change to societal, cultural, educational, or policy
responses (climate governance, activism, education, the arts) where a human, health, wellbeing,
or community dimension is plausibly present.

EXCLUDE only when none of the three routes is plausibly present -- for example a record with no
climate content at all, or a substance or topic present for a purely non-climate reason (a drug,
a single chemical studied only in vitro, an industrial-accident or safety hazard) with no
climate-and-health, mitigation, or adaptation angle.
